implementation_notes: C has no messaging primitives, so the whole structure is hand-written: the recipient set is an array of endpoint descriptors (a struct pairing a file descriptor or socket address with a name) resolved from configuration or the message, and the router is a loop that copies the payload and calls send(2)/sendmsg(2) - or write(2) - once per entry, recording each call's return value. What replaces the classic Channel and Router classes is simply a table plus a loop: the channel is the descriptor and the routing decision is an array index. The hand-written form stays justified only when the fan-out must live inside a constrained process (an edge gateway, broker shim or embedded agent) where no messaging library is available, and even then the recipient set should be loaded from data, not hard-coded.
pitfalls: A short write on a stream socket means the tail of the message never arrives; loop on the returned count or switch to sendmsg() for the whole record.
The endpoint table is shared mutable state: a router thread fanning out while another closes or reuses a descriptor races unless ownership and locking are defined.
There is no built-in flow control: a full socket buffer blocks the loop, so a single slow recipient halts the entire fan-out.
